title: Music store job and first professional band in Pensacola
summary: Includes working at a music store and playing first jobs with married men, backed by Black fraternal organizations in Pensacola.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: When did you start playing music professionally for, you know, your first few jobs?

Well I wasn't calling myself a professional before, before 24. I was in ninth grade, 35, right there, F1-0. And these two guys was taking lessons. This man and these guys were married men and everything. They left in the days first. The Trammer played George Morris, and Trump was played Thomas Mack. And the saxophone player, Edmund Washington. I just buried them this year, first part of this year. And they used to get a little job, they used to hire me. They had family and everything. I mean, they were work guys, married and everything. And so we got this job, a fellow named Joe Wynn came to, and he all in looking for a bang. He went up on the roof, Gordon, a couple other places. So he contacted, some way he contacted this guy, the one that worked with, he was sort of a porter at the Groom Hall or something like that, an old hotel. And so we used to get jobs, you know, on the weekends, like maybe Friday, Saturday, Sunday, like that. And so this man came to the, and he decided to take us. His name was Joe Wynn. He was just sort of a gambler and a son of a guy. He wasn't a help of a gentleman. I saw Peter Rayford, he was with us when we were to get jobs, you see. So we told him that when we were going, we couldn't take him, and he didn't like it. So we told him that if anything was possible that we were having trouble with this guy, we sent one. So it was a black organization. These people were very, I've seemed very proud of them, because we had them all down here. They were black masons, and they were in business. You know, they had them own property. A lot of them owned, had their own business. One of the doctors was, the doctor, the black doctor, and he had his own drugstore. This man, Aaron, had his own cab stand, had his own restaurant, and had his own meat shop. And there's this either Aaron Long and the doctor, and somebody else. And they had a park. In those days, most black cities, they had their own amusement park. They'd have their own baseball game, baseball team. That's what these people had in Pensacola. They had it in Mobile, I know. And Montgomery had the same thing. So I was making twenty-four dollars work. My dad was making about, I was working only three days a week. Sometimes they'd double or something, but they'd still pay the twenty-four dollars a whole lot of money. My daddy was making about fifteen to seventeen dollars working at the Pee's and the Temple. And then seven on Sunday, because the elevator man would take off. See? And we made a big hit. On Pensacola. We called it the Pensacola Jazz. See, during those times, there were people who would hire different bands from the Orient, because on account of the people who took a racket to the Orient Jazz Music. Mobile got popular with it. We had a black man named Gomez at Dennis. He opened up a place. They had places before him. You see? And those places did that to make money. They had the ground and everything. They were like a pavilion. I don't know if you know what the pavilion was. They had them out at the lake. They had them in some of the parks and everything where you could play. But these were owned by these people. The organization. And that was my biggest achievement in my success. In life, the song that I was going to be a musician, instead of playing the music. See?
